newsitem.title: UK: Fund managers neutral on UK shares - Merrill.
newsitem.headline: Fund managers neutral on UK shares - Merrill.

text.p: Fund managers are taking a neutral view towards UK shares, with a strong pound and fears of higher interest rates countering optimism on the outlook for economic growth, according to a poll by Merrill Lynch released on Monday.
"Managers in the UK and overseas are generally not looking to add to their UK equity exposure," Merrill said in its monthly fund managers survey.
"This probably reflects the universal view of UK respondents that base rates will rise over the coming year."
The survey found fund managers expected sterling's current strength to persist.

"As a result, managers are less keen on international sectors such as chemicals and pharmaceuticals where currency- related profit downgrades are most likely, and are looking to switch into domestic sectors such as food retailers and brewers," it said.

Chemicals and pharmaceuticals showed the strongest decline in favour over the last three months, with alcoholic beverages also suffering. Retailers, brewers and construction firms showed the biggest gain in sentiment.

The strength of sterling was also reflected in preferences for the less internationally-oriented FTSE 250 versus the FTSE 100. "Two-thirds of managers say they prefer the smaller FTSE 250 stocks, against only 55 percent last month," Merrill said.
It said the average forecast for UK economic growth was 3.4 percent in 1997 and 2.8 percent in 1998.
"This is reflected in respondents' increasing preference for commercial property and smaller companies, both of which tend to prosper when growth is strong," the survey said.

Among the funds surveyed, those planning to cut their holdings of UK equities outnumbered those planning to increase them by a majority of one, a slight improvement from the majority of four recorded in December and November.
Funds were continuing to increase European exposure, with a majority of 11 buyers over sellers compared with 18 in December.
"Continental Europe may be a better place to invest funds," said Merrill strategist Bijal Shah.
"Europe as a whole is beginning to show the first green shoots of an economic upswing. Corporate profits should rise and monetary policy is likely to remain benign."
The majority of funds turned bearish on Japan, with three more sellers than buyers compared with a 12-strong majority of buyers in December.
Wall Street continued to be regarded with caution, with a balance of 10 sellers over buyers versus nine in December.
Taken by pollsters Gallup between January 6 and 8, the survey polled 79 institutions controlling funds totalling $1,913 billion.
